clue.text: Invent a herb

definitions.meaning: to coin a new word or phrase
a common garden herb used in sauces and tea

explanation.walkthrough: Two short definitions sit side by side with no wordplay: coining a word and a kitchen herb share one name.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: to mint a phrase is to invent it, and mint is the familiar herb.

clue.text: Dodgy stimulator for agents of unwelcome change

indicators.note: dodgy means unsound or broken, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dubious device is blamed for making things worse.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole answer is in one word, a neat pairing of something that boosts with something that damages.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who mutilate bring about a change to something that nobody wanted.

clue.text: Tangled knotweed? No, only if necessary

definitions.note: need-to-know is used adjectivally, as in 'on a need-to-know basis', which the phrase paraphrases

indicators.note: tangled letters are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: A gardener faced with invasive knotweed decides to deal with it only when forced to.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'No' make the surface read as a conversation about weeding, but the NO is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Information given on a need-to-know basis is shared only when it is necessary.

clue.text: What may be seen in Manhattan is a film about greed

definitions.text: What may be seen in Manhattan
definitions.meaning: the financial district's street in lower Manhattan
Oliver Stone's 1987 film, home of 'greed is good'

explanation.surface: A tourist note that a film set in New York is about greed.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves point at the same place: the real street in New York and the film named after it, whose villain Gordon Gekko declares that greed is good.
explanation.definitionFit: Wall Street is a street in Manhattan and the title of a well-known film about greed.

clue.text: After injection of iodine, a thorax is most sore

indicators.note: an injection puts something inside

parts.note: I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: A medical note that after an iodine injection the patient's chest hurts most.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes the injection sound like treatment; it is the instruction to put I inside CHEST, after the leading A.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to ache is to be sore, and the superlative ending matches 'most'.

clue.text: Large prison officers failing to open smallish rooms

indicators.note: the officers' word loses the letter that would open it

parts.note: L = large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Big prison guards cannot unlock the doors of some small rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failing to open' looks like a stuck cell door, and it removes the opening letter W from WARDERS.
explanation.definitionFit: A larder is a small room or cupboard for storing food.

clue.text: Leading lady to see where appetisers appear

definitions.note: top of the bill names the star act, here a person
definitions.meaning: the star performer, named first on a theatre poster
starters are listed first on a restaurant check

explanation.surface: A night out: a show with a star, then a restaurant with starters.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre bill (the poster listing the acts) and the restaurant bill share a name, and both put the headline item at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: The performer at the top of the bill is the headline act, the one everyone comes to see.

clue.text: Disasters Leonidas dodged regularly

indicators.note: every other letter is dodged, so only alternate letters remain

explanation.surface: The Spartan king Leonidas repeatedly escaped catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: Leonidas is the Spartan king who died at Thermopylae, so the surface has irony, but he is only a string of letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: An end, in the sense of a violent death or ruin, is a disaster.

clue.text: Country 15?
We're told of SE Asians' connections

indicators.note: what we are told is heard, so the answer sounds like the wordplay

parts.note: Thais, people of Thailand in Southeast Asia

explanation.surface: A report about the links between people in Southeast Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe on 'Asians’' makes the surface read as a possessive; it is just the plural sounded out.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: bonds or links between people, as in family ties.

clue.text: Goth prayed desperately for source of support

indicators.note: desperate action is wild, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: A troubled Goth prays hard for help.
explanation.walkthrough: The Goth wants help in the surface and gets it in the answer, an animal brought in to comfort people.
explanation.definitionFit: A therapy dog is brought to hospitals and schools to comfort and support people.

clue.text: Funny, mirthful Noel, OK?

indicators.note: funny means odd, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a cheerful comedian called Noel is actually any good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' and 'mirthful' both read as praise for a comic, and 'OK?' looks like a question to him; it is the definition, OK in the sense of merely adequate.
explanation.definitionFit: Something run-of-the-mill is ordinary, just OK; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Greens' constituent circulated cute leaflet

indicators.note: letters sent round are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A local member of the Green Party hands round an appealing leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greens’ constituent' reads as a voter for the Green Party; it means one part of a plate of salad greens.
explanation.definitionFit: Part for whole: salad greens are made of leaves, and this is one of them.

clue.text: Everyman regularly gets into these arguments

definitions.meaning: Everyman is the setter of this weekly puzzle
split as two words: angry words exchanged in a row

explanation.surface: The setter admits to getting into rows often.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is this puzzle's setter and appears in the Observer every week, so he is regularly in these puzzles. 'Regularly' is not taking alternate letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross words exchanged in anger make an argument, and Everyman's grids appear weekly.

clue.text: Incites, in middle of open court, displays of fury

indicators.note: only the letters in the middle of the phrase are taken

parts.note: the middle five of OPENCOURT: op-ENCOU-rt

explanation.surface: Someone stirs up angry scenes in the middle of a public court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open court' reads as a legal term; it is simply nine letters whose centre runs across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: To encourage someone to act can be to incite them.

clue.text: Murder a pizza?

definitions.meaning: a meal bought to eat elsewhere; the question mark says a pizza is only an example

explanation.surface: A gangster's order that could be a hit or a dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb 'take out' is gangster slang for kill; the noun is the delivery meal.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone out is to murder them, and a pizza is a typical takeout.

clue.text: Very hot Norwegians, A-ha: randy (to some extent)

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the answer is inside it

explanation.surface: The Norwegian pop band A-ha are said to be hot and lustful.
explanation.walkthrough: A-ha, the Norwegian band behind 'Take On Me', make the surface plausible; the hyphen and punctuation are ignored in reading the letters through.
explanation.definitionFit: Saharan heat, like that of the Sahara desert, is extreme.

clue.text: List includes duck — but you want another bird …

indicators.note: the list holds the duck inside it

parts.note: a roster is a list of names
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O

explanation.surface: A list includes a duck, but the reader asks for a different bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is a bird in the surface, which is why the definition says 'another bird', but in the wordplay it is a cricket score of zero, O. The ellipsis leads on into 19 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male chicken, a different bird from a duck.

clue.text: Cooked but not good: dotted with holes

indicators.note: the letter named after it is left out

explanation.surface: Some food was cooked badly and came out full of holes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not good' reads as a verdict on the cooking; it is an instruction to delete G from GRIDDLED.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: perforated all over, as a riddle, an old word for a coarse sieve, is.

clue.text: … a small company, and you want credit note up-front? Sauce!

indicators.note: the credit note goes at the front of the rest

parts.note: a tab is a running record of credit at a bar
S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Continuing from 17 across: someone in a small firm wants an advance on credit, which is cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to 17 across. 'Sauce!' with its exclamation mark reads as 'What cheek!'; it is the definition, the hot sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabasco is a brand of hot pepper sauce.

clue.text: Lad caught by Dorothy's dog somewhere in N America

indicators.note: the lad is held inside the dog's name

parts.note: Toto, Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz

explanation.surface: A boy is grabbed by Toto, the dog from The Wizard of Oz, somewhere in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorothy and her dog point to Kansas, but the city is in Canada; any boy's name can stand for 'lad'.
explanation.definitionFit: Toronto is a city in Canada, so in North America.

clue.text: Cockney retained her provision for baking — and something for liqueurs?

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the H, so the words are heard in that accent

parts.note: HELD HER with Cockney dropped Hs, then flour, a baker's staple

explanation.surface: A Londoner kept back her baking supplies, with a nod to making liqueurs.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the London working-class accent known for dropping H, so 'held her flour' comes out as the answer. The question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderflowers are used to flavour cordials and liqueurs such as St-Germain.

clue.text: Tosses in a turgid offhand prècis … finally

indicators.note: each word gives its final letter

parts.note: the final letters of A turgiD offhanD prècisS

explanation.surface: A writer throws a few things into a dull, careless summary at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The single-letter word 'a' counts: its last letter is its only letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To toss something in is to add it, as when adding an extra.

clue.text: America is a revolutionary, enormous mass of land

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: A = America, as in USA. The same letters also run on unbroken across neighbouring clue words, a coincidence of the pieces sitting side by side; the setter gives no hidden-word signal.

explanation.surface: A statement that America is a radical, vast continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' reads as describing America's history, and it turns the whole string round.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the largest continent is the most enormous landmass there is.

clue.text: Thomas perhaps embracing trendy field of research

indicators.note: an embrace holds something inside

parts.note: Thomas was one of the twelve disciples

explanation.surface: Someone called Thomas takes up a fashionable area of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thomas perhaps' is a definition by example: Doubting Thomas was one of Jesus's twelve followers. The surface makes Thomas sound like a student picking a subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Academic sense: a branch of learning, such as a field in which research is done.

clue.text: 'A bore'? Tolkien creature? That's not on

indicators.note: the letters ON are not there

parts.note: Smaug in The Hobbit is a dragon

explanation.surface: Someone calls a Tolkien monster boring and complains that it is unacceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's not on' is the British phrase for 'that is unacceptable', and it removes ON from DRAGON.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: something tedious is a drag, just as it is a bore.

clue.text: Daffy old boater's one swinging more than one way

definitions.text: one swinging more than one way

indicators.note: daffy means scatty, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A silly old boating man is a swinger.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S in 'boater’s' looks like 'boater is' and supplies the S of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A stable door is split into top and bottom halves that swing open independently.

clue.text: Judas Iscariot, within: unaltered

indicators.note: the answer is inside the words

explanation.surface: Judas Iscariot is inside and unchanged.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the break between the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods sold as is are sold unaltered, in their present state.
